sections.name: Blender Interface & Fundamentals
sections.explanation_simple: Blender is like a spaceship control panel - intimidating at first, but every button has a purpose. The 3D Viewport is your main window, the Timeline at the bottom is for animation, the Outliner on the right shows everything in your scene, and the Properties panel on the far right controls settings. The most important thing to learn is the keyboard shortcuts: G = Grab (move), R = Rotate, S = Scale, Tab = Toggle Edit Mode. These shortcuts make Blender 10x faster once you memorize them.
key_concepts: 3D Viewport: Main window where you create and see your 3D world
Outliner: List of every object in your scene
Properties Panel: Controls for objects, materials, render settings
Timeline: For animation (keyframes and scrubbing)
Object Mode: Move/rotate/scale whole objects
Edit Mode: Edit the vertices, edges, and faces of a mesh
Sculpt Mode: Push/pull clay digitally
Tab Key: Toggle between Object and Edit Mode
G: Grab (move), R: Rotate, S: Scale
X: Delete, E: Extrude, Ctrl+R: Loop Cut, K: Knife Tool

code_examples.title: Basic Navigation and Keyboard Shortcuts
code_examples.code:
/*
BLENDER NAVIGATION CHEATSHEET

=== VIEWPORT NAVIGATION ===
Middle Mouse Button: Orbit camera
Shift + Middle Mouse: Pan camera
Scroll: Zoom in/out
Numpad 1: Front view
Numpad 3: Right view
Numpad 7: Top view
Numpad 0: Camera view
Numpad 5: Toggle perspective/orthographic

=== BASIC TRANSFORMS ===
G: Move (Grab)
R: Rotate
S: Scale
After pressing G/R/S:
  X/Y/Z: Lock to axis
  Shift+X/Y/Z: Lock out of axis
  Number: Precise value (G X 5 moves 5 units on X)

=== SELECTION ===
Right-click: Select
A: Select/Deselect all
B: Box select
C: Circle select (scroll to resize)
Alt+Right-click: Select edge loop
Ctrl+I: Invert selection
H: Hide selected
Alt+H: Unhide all

=== EDITING ===
Tab: Toggle Edit Mode
1/2/3: Vertex/Edge/Face select mode
E: Extrude
I: Inset
Ctrl+R: Loop cut
K: Knife tool (Enter to confirm)
Ctrl+B: Bevel
F: Fill (make face from selected edges)
X: Delete menu
M: Merge
P: Separate selection to new object

=== MODIFIERS ===
The most commonly used modifiers:
- Subdivision Surface: Smooths mesh by subdividing faces
- Mirror: Mirrors mesh across axis (for symmetrical modeling)
- Bevel: Rounds sharp edges
- Array: Creates a grid/line of copies
- Solidify: Gives thickness to thin surfaces
- Boolean: Add/Subtract/Intersect with another mesh
- Displace: Deforms mesh based on texture
*/

// Blender Python API equivalent of manual operations
import bpy

# Add a cube
bpy.ops.mesh.primitive_cube_add(size=2, location=(0, 0, 0))

# Get reference to the new cube
cube = bpy.context.active_object

# Switch to edit mode
bpy.ops.object.mode_set(mode='EDIT')

# Subdivide all faces
bpy.ops.mesh.subdivide(number_cuts=2)

# Switch back to object mode
bpy.ops.object.mode_set(mode='OBJECT')

# Add subdivision surface modifier
mod = cube.modifiers.new(name="Subdivision", type='SUBSURF')
mod.levels = 2
mod.render_levels = 3

# Smooth shading
bpy.ops.object.shade_smooth()

sections.learning_path: Learn the interface -> Memorize G/R/S/Tab -> Practice basic modeling -> Learn modifiers -> Learn materials and lighting

sections.name: Mesh Modeling (Hard Surface & Organic)
sections.explanation_simple: Mesh modeling is building 3D objects by manipulating vertices (points), edges (lines between points), and faces (flat surfaces). Hard surface modeling is for man-made objects like guns, cars, buildings, and robots - these have sharp edges and flat surfaces. Organic modeling is for living things like characters, animals, and creatures - these have smooth curves and flowing forms. Both start from simple shapes (cube, sphere, cylinder) that you push, pull, cut, and extrude into the final form.
key_concepts: Vertices: Points in 3D space (the 'corners' of your model)
Edges: Lines connecting two vertices
Faces: Flat surfaces made of 3+ edges (triangles or quads)
Extrude (E): Pull a face outward to create new geometry
Loop Cut (Ctrl+R): Add a ring of edges around the mesh
Bevel (Ctrl+B): Round off sharp edges
Boolean: Cut one shape from another (like cookie cutters)
Mirror Modifier: Model half, get the other half for free
Subdivision Surface: Makes low-poly models smooth (game changer)
Edge Flow: How edges follow the shape of your model

code_examples.title: Blender Python: Create a Hard Surface Sci-Fi Panel
code_examples.code:
import bpy
import math

# Clear existing objects
bpy.ops.object.select_all(action='SELECT')
bpy.ops.object.delete(use_global=False)

# Create the base panel
bpy.ops.mesh.primitive_cube_add(size=2, location=(0, 0, 0))
panel = bpy.context.active_object
panel.name = "SciFi_Panel"

# Scale to make it flat
panel.scale = (3, 2, 0.2)
bpy.ops.object.transform_apply(scale=True)

# Enter edit mode and make insets
bpy.ops.object.mode_set(mode='EDIT')
bpy.ops.mesh.select_mode(type='FACE')

# Select top and bottom faces (they're facing Z)
bpy.ops.mesh.select_all(action='DESELECT')
bpy.ops.view3d.select_pattern(extend=False, pattern="*Z*")

# Inset to create panel border
bpy.ops.mesh.inset(thickness=0.1, depth=0)

# Inset again for inner panel
bpy.ops.mesh.inset(thickness=0.05, depth=-0.05)

# Add some detail cuts
bpy.ops.mesh.select_mode(type='EDGE')
bpy.ops.mesh.select_all(action='DESELECT')
# Add loop cuts for detail (would do manually in real workflow)

bpy.ops.object.mode_set(mode='OBJECT')

# Add bevel modifier for the sci-fi look
bevel = panel.modifiers.new(name="Bevel", type='BEVEL')
bevel.width = 0.02
bevel.segments = 3

# Add subdivision surface for smoothness
subdiv = panel.modifiers.new(name="Subdivision", type='SUBSURF')
subdiv.levels = 1
subdiv.render_levels = 2

# Create material
mat = bpy.data.materials.new(name="SciFi_Metal")
mat.use_nodes = True
nodes = mat.node_tree.nodes
links = mat.node_tree.links

# Clear default nodes
nodes.clear()

# Add Principled BSDF
principled = nodes.new(type='ShaderNodeBsdfPrincipled')
principled.inputs['Base Color'].default_value = (0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 1)
principled.inputs['Metallic'].default_value = 0.8
principled.inputs['Roughness'].default_value = 0.3
principled.inputs['Emission'].default_value = (0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1)
principled.inputs['Emission Strength'].default_value = 0.5

output = nodes.new(type='ShaderNodeOutputMaterial')
links.new(principled.outputs['BSDF'], output.inputs['Surface'])

panel.data.materials.append(mat)

# Add lighting
bpy.ops.object.light_add(type='AREA', location=(5, 5, 8))
light = bpy.context.active_object
light.data.energy = 1000

# Add camera
bpy.ops.object.camera_add(location=(6, -4, 3))
cam = bpy.context.active_object
cam.rotation_euler = (math.radians(60), 0, math.radians(45))
bpy.context.scene.camera = cam

print("Sci-Fi panel created successfully!")

sections.learning_path: Basic shapes (cube, sphere, cylinder) -> Edit mode (E, Ctrl+R, Ctrl+B) -> Modifiers (Mirror, Subdivide, Bevel) -> Hard surface workflow -> Organic modeling -> Retopology

sections.name: Sculpting & Organic Creation
sections.explanation_simple: Digital sculpting is like working with real clay, but with undo and unlimited clay. Instead of pushing individual vertices, you use brushes that affect areas of the mesh like real sculpting tools. A Clay brush adds volume, a Crease brush makes sharp lines, an Inflate brush puffs things up. Sculpting is the fastest way to create organic shapes like characters, creatures, and terrain. You start with a simple sphere and 'mold' it into a face, body, or monster.
key_concepts: Dyntopo: Dynamic topology - adds/subtracts polygons as you sculpt
Multiresolution: Multiple detail levels (sculpt low-poly, then add finer detail)
Clay Brush: Adds volume like adding clay
Crease Brush: Carves sharp lines (wrinkles, muscles)
Snake Hook: Pulls clay out (noses, ears, horns)
Smooth Brush: Softens rough areas
Masking: Protect areas from sculpting
Symmetry: Left/right mirror (sculpt one side, get both)
VDM Brushes: Pre-made sculpting shapes (eyes, noses) you can stamp on
Remesh: Rebuild clean topology from sculpt

code_examples.title: Blender Python: Sculpt a Simple Head
code_examples.code:
import bpy
import math

# Clear scene
bpy.ops.object.select_all(action='SELECT')
bpy.ops.object.delete(use_global=False)

# Add a base sphere
bpy.ops.mesh.primitive_uv_sphere_add(radius=1, location=(0, 0, 0))
head = bpy.context.active_object
head.name = "Head_Base"

# Add multiresolution modifier for sculpting
multires = head.modifiers.new(name="Multires", type='MULTIRES')
multires.levels = 0
multires.total_levels = 6

# Subdivide a few levels for detail
for i in range(4):
    bpy.ops.object.multires_subdivide(modifier="Multires")

# Enter sculpt mode
bpy.ops.object.mode_set(mode='SCULPT')

# Set symmetry
head.use_mesh_mirror_x = True

# Basic sculpting operations (would do manually, but here's API)
# The following would be done by hand with a tablet:
# 1. Use Clay brush to build cheekbones
# 2. Use Crease brush to define eye sockets
# 3. Use Snake Hook to pull out nose
# 4. Use Crease for mouth line
# 5. Smooth brush to blend everything

print("Head base ready for sculpting!")
print("Switch to Sculpt Mode and use these brushes:")
print("  - Clay: Build form (cheeks, chin, brow)")
print("  - Crease: Define features (eyes, mouth, nose)")
print("  - Snake Hook: Pull out nose, ears")
print("  - Smooth: Blend and soften")

sections.learning_path: Sculpt mode basics -> Brush types and settings -> Dyntopo vs Multires -> Symmetry sculpting -> Anatomy study -> Detailing -> Retopology for animation

sections.name: Texturing & Materials
sections.explanation_simple: Texturing is how you give color and detail to your 3D models. A plain white cube becomes a rusty metal box, a smooth rock, or a glowing crystal just by changing the material. The most powerful material in Blender is the Principled BSDF - it can create ANY real-world surface. You control things like Base Color (what color is it), Metallic (is it metal?), Roughness (how shiny?), and Normal Map (bumpy details without changing the mesh). Textures are images that control these properties.
key_concepts: Principled BSDF: The 'all-in-one' material node that does everything
Base Color: The main color/albedo of the surface
Metallic: 0 = non-metal (wood, plastic, skin), 1 = metal (iron, gold)
Roughness: 0 = mirror smooth, 1 = completely rough (sandpaper)
Normal Map: Fake bumps and dents without changing geometry
Displacement Map: Actually moves vertices (real bumps, needs subdivision)
UV Unwrapping: Flattening 3D surface onto 2D image (like peeling an orange)
Texture Paint: Painting directly on the 3D model
Procedural Textures: Math-generated textures (no image file needed)
PBR: Physically Based Rendering - realistic materials that react naturally to light

code_examples.title: Blender Python: Create PBR Material with Nodes
code_examples.code:
import bpy
import os

def create_pbr_material(name, base_color, metallic=0, roughness=0.5):
    """Create a PBR material with procedural textures."""
    mat = bpy.data.materials.new(name=name)
    mat.use_nodes = True
    nodes = mat.node_tree.nodes
    links = mat.node_tree.links
    
    # Clear default
    nodes.clear()
    
    # Create output
    output = nodes.new(type='ShaderNodeOutputMaterial')
    output.location = (400, 0)
    
    # Create Principled BSDF
    principled = nodes.new(type='ShaderNodeBsdfPrincipled')
    principled.location = (0, 0)
    principled.inputs['Base Color'].default_value = (*base_color, 1)
    principled.inputs['Metallic'].default_value = metallic
    principled.inputs['Roughness'].default_value = roughness
    
    # Connect
    links.new(principled.outputs['BSDF'], output.inputs['Surface'])
    
    # Add procedural noise for detail (if not fully metallic)
    if metallic < 0.5:
        # Noise texture for roughness variation
        noise = nodes.new(type='ShaderNodeTexNoise')
        noise.location = (-300, -200)
        noise.inputs['Scale'].default_value = 5
        noise.inputs['Detail'].default_value = 3
        noise.inputs['Roughness'].default_value = 0.5
        
        # Color ramp to control the noise output
        ramp = nodes.new(type='ShaderNodeValToRGB')
        ramp.location = (-100, -200)
        links.new(noise.outputs['Fac'], ramp.inputs['Fac'])
        
        # Mix roughness
        mix = nodes.new(type='ShaderNodeMixRGB')
        mix.location = (100, -200)
        mix.blend_type = 'MIX'
        links.new(ramp.outputs['Color'], mix.inputs['Fac'])
        mix.inputs['Color1'].default_value = (roughness, roughness, roughness, 1)
        mix.inputs['Color2'].default_value = (min(roughness + 0.3, 1),) * 3 + (1,)
        links.new(mix.outputs['Color'], principled.inputs['Roughness'])
    
    return mat

# Create materials for different purposes
metal_mat = create_pbr_material("Gold_Metal", (0.8, 0.6, 0.1), metallic=1.0, roughness=0.1)
wood_mat = create_pbr_material("Wood", (0.4, 0.25, 0.1), metallic=0, roughness=0.7)
plastic_mat = create_pbr_material("Red_Plastic", (0.8, 0.1, 0.1), metallic=0, roughness=0.3)

# Apply material to active object
if bpy.context.active_object:
    obj = bpy.context.active_object
    if obj.data.materials:
        obj.data.materials[0] = metal_mat
    else:
        obj.data.materials.append(metal_mat)
    
print(f"Created materials: Gold_Metal, Wood, Red_Plastic")
print(f"Applied {metal_mat.name} to {obj.name}")

sections.learning_path: Principled BSDF basics -> Color, metallic, roughness -> Texture images (download or paint) -> UV unwrapping -> Procedural textures (nodes) -> PBR workflows -> Substance integration

sections.name: Animation & Rigging
sections.explanation_simple: Rigging is building a digital skeleton inside a character so you can animate it. Think of it like a puppet: the strings attach to specific points on the puppet, and when you pull them, the puppet moves. In 3D, the 'strings' are bones connected in a hierarchy. A leg bone connects to a foot bone, which connects to the body. When you rotate the thigh bone, the whole leg moves naturally. Weight painting controls WHICH parts of the mesh move with each bone (move the arm bone, the bicep and forearm should follow, but the chest should not).
key_concepts: Armature: The skeleton (collection of bones)
Bone: A single bone in the skeleton
Bone Hierarchy: Parent-child relationships (upper arm -> lower arm -> hand)
IK (Inverse Kinematics): Move hand, arm adjusts automatically
FK (Forward Kinematics): Rotate each bone individually (for arcs and swings)
Weight Painting: How much each bone affects each vertex (0-1 range)
Vertex Groups: Lists of vertices assigned to each bone
Pose Mode: Mode for animating the rig
Action: A single animation (walk, run, jump)
NLA (Non-Linear Animation): Layering multiple animations (walk + wave)

code_examples.title: Blender Python: Create a Simple Arm Rig
code_examples.code:
import bpy
import math

def create_arm_rig(name="Arm_Rig"):
    """Create a simple arm with IK/FK support."""
    # Create armature
    bpy.ops.object.armature_add(enter_editmode=True, location=(0, 0, 0))
    armature = bpy.context.active_object
    armature.name = name
    
    # Get the armature data
    amt = armature.data
    amt.display_type = 'WIRE'
    
    # Delete default bone
    bpy.ops.armature.select_all(action='SELECT')
    bpy.ops.armature.delete()
    
    # Create bones in edit mode
    # Upper arm
    bpy.ops.armature.bone_primitive_add(name="UpperArm")
    upper = amt.edit_bones["UpperArm"]
    upper.head = (0, 0, 0)
    upper.tail = (0, 0, 1.5)
    
    # Lower arm
    bpy.ops.armature.bone_primitive_add(name="Forearm")
    forearm = amt.edit_bones["Forearm"]
    forearm.head = (0, 0, 1.5)
    forearm.tail = (0, 0, 3.0)
    forearm.parent = upper
    
    # Hand
    bpy.ops.armature.bone_primitive_add(name="Hand")
    hand = amt.edit_bones["Hand"]
    hand.head = (0, 0, 3.0)
    hand.tail = (0, 0.3, 3.5)
    hand.parent = forearm
    
    # IK target bone
    bpy.ops.armature.bone_primitive_add(name="IK_Target")
    ik = amt.edit_bones["IK_Target"]
    ik.head = (0, 0.5, 3.0)
    ik.tail = (0, 1.0, 3.5)
    
    # Return to object mode
    bpy.ops.object.mode_set(mode='OBJECT')
    
    return armature

# Create the rig
rig = create_arm_rig()

# Add IK constraint
bpy.ops.object.mode_set(mode='POSE')

# Get the forearm bone and add IK constraint
forearm = rig.pose.bones["Forearm"]
ik_constraint = forearm.constraints.new(type='IK')
ik_constraint.target = rig
ik_constraint.subtarget = "IK_Target"
ik_constraint.chain_count = 2

bpy.ops.object.mode_set(mode='OBJECT')

print(f"Arm rig '{rig.name}' created with IK system!")
print("Switch to Pose Mode and move IK_Target to pose the arm.")

sections.learning_path: Armature basics -> Bone placement -> FK animation -> IK systems -> Weight painting -> Character rigging -> Animation principles (12 principles) -> NLA editor
